discovery: Theory of crackling noise: universal avalanche dynamics and depinning transitions in disordered systems
subfield: Statistical physics of disordered systems / non-equilibrium critical phenomena
motivation: Many driven disordered systems respond not smoothly but in intermittent bursts: Barkhausen noise in magnets, crystal plasticity, fracture, earthquakes, fluid fronts in porous media. Fisher showed that elastic interfaces pinned by quenched disorder undergo a genuine dynamical critical transition (depinning), and developed its renormalization-group theory. Sethna and Dahmen, through the random-field Ising model of hysteresis and the 'crackling noise' framework, showed that avalanche size distributions, durations and even average avalanche shapes are universal, scale-invariant and quantitatively predictable. Their mean-field and RG predictions have since been confirmed in experiments on magnets, micropillar plasticity, metallic glasses and granular and porous media. Together these contributions turned noise in messy materials from a nuisance into a precise probe of non-equilibrium criticality, and they give a unified, predictive physics of how disordered matter yields, slips and breaks.
